description: Physical streaming replication as the selected node sees it: cluster-wide per-standby lag, a selected standby's lag across all four stages (sent, write, flush, replay) in bytes and time, WAL generation, and whether each standby sends hot standby feedback.

panels.description: Number of walsender connections currently visible in pg_stat_replication on this node (pg_basebackup / pg_rewind sessions excluded). A drop to 0 means every standby has disconnected — the row simply disappears from pg_stat_replication, it does not linger with a large lag. This overview stays cluster-wide when the Standby selector changes.
panels.title: Connected standbys

panels.description: Worst replay lag over the same trailing `$__rate_interval` window as *Replay lag per standby (time)*, so it matches that graph's right-hand endpoint. This is the user-visible staleness of a read replica. Empty on an idle, fully caught-up primary because PostgreSQL reverts these interval columns to NULL rather than zero. This overview stays cluster-wide when the Standby selector changes.
panels.title: Replay lag now (time)

panels.description: Worst replay lag over the same trailing `$__rate_interval` window as *Replay lag per standby (bytes)*, so it matches that graph's right-hand endpoint. This is the distance in WAL bytes between `pg_current_wal_lsn()` here and any standby's `replay_lsn`. Bytes and time should agree unless the time columns went NULL on an idle system while the byte distance stayed real. This overview stays cluster-wide when the Standby selector changes.
panels.title: Replay lag now (bytes)

panels.description: Standbys whose `sync_state` is `sync` or `quorum`. 0 with a non-empty `synchronous_standby_names` means the intended synchronous standby is not currently eligible, and commits may be waiting. This overview stays cluster-wide when the Standby selector changes.
panels.title: Synchronous standbys

panels.description: Standbys currently reporting a non-null `backend_xmin` in pg_stat_replication. A non-null `backend_xmin` is primary-side evidence that the standby runs with `hot_standby_feedback = on`. A standby with feedback on but no active read query can report null, so 0 means "no feedback observed", not certainly "feedback is off". This overview stays cluster-wide when the Standby selector changes.
panels.title: Standbys with feedback

panels.description: Current WAL timeline of this node. A timeline increment means a promotion happened — after a failover every standby that was not rewound or re-cloned will stop following this node.
panels.title: Timeline

panels.description: `pg_current_wal_lsn() − replay_lsn` per standby: the WAL each standby still has to apply. This cluster-wide comparison stays unchanged when the Standby selector changes; the selector controls the detail and per-standby health rows below. Standby identity is `application_name`; client address and port are intentionally aggregated so reconnects continue the same line. Plotted as the maximum over a trailing `$__rate_interval` window so short stalls survive downsampling.
panels.title: Replay lag per standby (bytes)

panels.description: `pg_stat_replication.replay_lag` per standby: how long the standby took to confirm it had applied recently flushed WAL — the delay `synchronous_commit = remote_apply` would have paid. Plotted as the maximum over a trailing `$__rate_interval` window so short stalls survive downsampling. This cluster-wide comparison stays unchanged when the Standby selector changes. Standby identity is `application_name`; client address and port are intentionally aggregated so reconnects continue the same line. **Gaps are meaningful**: PostgreSQL reverts these columns to NULL once a standby is fully caught up on an idle primary, so a gap means 'caught up and idle'. Also inflated by `recovery_min_apply_delay`, which is deliberate.
panels.title: Replay lag per standby (time)

panels.description: Select one standby to see where its WAL is stuck: the replay gap is split at `pg_current_wal_lsn() → sent_lsn → write_lsn → flush_lsn → replay_lsn` into four additive stage bands. The tall stacked band names the bottleneck: band 2 → network or walreceiver; band 3 → standby WAL disk; band 4 → apply. Band 1 is WAL written since the last status message, so judge whether it grows. The whole displayed range must contain exactly one `application_name`. Two physical senders sharing a name are treated as one and may blend; use unique `application_name` values.

defaults.noValue: select one standby to analyze replication stages

targets.expr: (clamp_min(max_over_time((pgwatch_replication_write_lag_b{cluster="$cluster_name", node_name="$node_name", application_name=~"$replica"} - pgwatch_replication_sent_lag_b{cluster="$cluster_name", node_name="$node_name", application_name=~"$replica"})[$__rate_interval]), 0)) and on() (count(count by (application_name) (max_over_time(pgwatch_replication_replay_lag_b{cluster="$cluster_name", node_name="$node_name", application_name=~"$replica"}[$__range]))) == 1)
targets.legendFormat: 2. sent, not written: sent_lsn − write_lsn (network / walreceiver)

targets.expr: (clamp_min(max_over_time((pgwatch_replication_flush_lag_b{cluster="$cluster_name", node_name="$node_name", application_name=~"$replica"} - pgwatch_replication_write_lag_b{cluster="$cluster_name", node_name="$node_name", application_name=~"$replica"})[$__rate_interval]), 0)) and on() (count(count by (application_name) (max_over_time(pgwatch_replication_replay_lag_b{cluster="$cluster_name", node_name="$node_name", application_name=~"$replica"}[$__range]))) == 1)
targets.legendFormat: 3. written, not flushed: write_lsn − flush_lsn (standby fsync)

targets.expr: (clamp_min(max_over_time((pgwatch_replication_replay_lag_b{cluster="$cluster_name", node_name="$node_name", application_name=~"$replica"} - pgwatch_replication_flush_lag_b{cluster="$cluster_name", node_name="$node_name", application_name=~"$replica"})[$__rate_interval]), 0)) and on() (count(count by (application_name) (max_over_time(pgwatch_replication_replay_lag_b{cluster="$cluster_name", node_name="$node_name", application_name=~"$replica"}[$__range]))) == 1)
targets.legendFormat: 4. flushed, not replayed: flush_lsn − replay_lsn (standby apply)

panels.title: Replay lag by stage (bytes)

panels.description: Select one standby to compare `write_lag`, `flush_lag`, and `replay_lag`: these are cumulative, not additive commit costs, so they are deliberately not stacked or differenced. Gaps mean fully caught up and idle. The whole displayed range must contain exactly one `application_name`. Two physical senders sharing a name are treated as one and may blend; use unique `application_name` values.

defaults.noValue: select one standby to analyze replication stages

panels.title: Replay lag by stage (time)

panels.description: Left axis: how fast this node advances `pg_current_wal_lsn()` — the load every standby must keep up with. Right axis: the worst replay lag across all standbys. This cluster-wide correlation stays unchanged when the Standby selector changes. Lag rising only with WAL generation suggests a standby undersized for the write rate; episodes while WAL generation is flat point to the standby. Note that `irate` on the LSN fabricates one spike at a timeline switch; ignore that point.
panels.title: WAL generation rate vs replay lag

panels.description: Share of each hour each standby spent staler than `$lag_alert_s` seconds, counted from 1-minute samples. This is the number to compare against whatever staleness the application actually tolerates, and the one to alert on — instantaneous lag panels hide short, frequent stalls. Each point is 'minutes staler than `$lag_alert_s` in the preceding hour'. Minutes where the standby reported nothing (disconnected, or NULL on idle) are not counted; pair it with *Connected standbys*. Standby identity is `application_name`; client address and port are intentionally aggregated before thresholding so reconnects contribute to one series. This panel stays cluster-wide when the Standby selector changes.
panels.title: Minutes per hour above the replay-lag threshold
Hot standby feedback and xmin horizon

panels.description: 1 while the selected standby reports a non-null `backend_xmin` in pg_stat_replication, 0 otherwise. A steady 1 proves hot standby feedback is on; a steady 0 across busy periods is strong evidence it is off, though a standby with no active read can report null. With feedback off, snapshot recovery conflicts are enabled; with it on, the standby pins this node's cleanup horizon and may increase bloat. Standby identity is `application_name`; client address and port are intentionally aggregated across reconnects. This per-standby health panel follows the Standby selector; the overview and summary rows stay cluster-wide.
panels.title: Hot standby feedback per standby

panels.description: `age(backend_xmin)` for the selected standby: how far back a feedback-sending standby holds this node's cleanup horizon. Zero means the standby is not currently pinning anything. Large and growing means a long-running standby query is blocking vacuum here; dashboard 07 shows the same replication-sourced xmin horizon pressure. Standby identity is `application_name`; client address and port are intentionally aggregated across reconnects. This per-standby health panel follows the Standby selector; the overview and summary rows stay cluster-wide.
panels.title: Standby xmin age, in transactions

panels.description: Age of `reply_time` for the selected standby. A healthy standby stays in the low tens of seconds; frozen replay lag while this climbs means the standby stopped answering rather than replaying slowly. **Requires PostgreSQL 12+**, so this panel is empty on PG11. The dashed line is `wal_sender_timeout` on this node (primary), read from the raw millisecond setting with an explicit unit. Standby identity is `application_name`; client address and port are intentionally aggregated across reconnects. This per-standby health panel follows the Standby selector; the overview and summary rows stay cluster-wide.
panels.title: Time since the standby last replied

panels.description: One row per walsender connection visible in `pg_stat_replication`, with `application_name`, `usename`, client address and port, and last replay lag in bytes. This is intentionally the one per-connection panel: physical connection identity is `application_name` plus `client_info`, because two simultaneous senders sharing an application name must remain distinguishable. `state` and `sync_state` are carried as labels, so they appear as columns here. Use this cluster-wide table to identify every physical connection in the graphs; it stays unchanged when the Standby selector changes. The client port, state, and sync state can each start a new series when they change.
panels.title: Standby connections

panels.description: These are `$node_name`'s (the primary's) replication settings, as last sampled in the selected range. `synchronous_standby_names` decides which standby the `sync_state` column above reflects; `wal_keep_size` and `max_slot_wal_keep_size` bound how far a standby may fall behind before it can no longer catch up. Standby-side settings such as `hot_standby_feedback`, `max_standby_streaming_delay`, and `recovery_min_apply_delay` must be read on the standby itself; the per-standby **Hot standby feedback** panel is the only primary-side evidence for feedback. `wal_keep_size` and `max_slot_wal_keep_size` require PostgreSQL 13+; below that version, those rows are absent.
panels.title: Replication settings on the primary (sending side)
